abstract:
In targeted proteomics utilizing Selected Reaction Monitoring
(SRM),
the precise detection of specific peptides within complex mixtures
remains a significant challenge, particularly due to noise and interference
in chromatograms. Existing methodologies, such as isotopic labeling
and scoring algorithms, offer partial solutions but are constrained
by high run times and elevated false discovery rates. To address these
limitations, we have developed ProPickML a machine learning-based
tool designed to accurately identify peptide peaks across diverse
data sets, independent of the assumed presence of the peptide. This
model was trained on a manually labeled data set and subsequently
validated to assess its predictive accuracy. The results demonstrate
that the model reliably identifies peptide peaks in the presence of
noise, achieving a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.81
on an independent test data set, surpassing mProphet’s MCC
of 0.71. Implemented in R as ProPickML, this tool offers a competitive,
cost-effective alternative to existing techniques, significantly reducing
reliance on isotopic labeling and enhancing the accuracy of peptide
identification in SRM workflows.

Materials and Method
Data Acquisition
To train the machine learning models
and evaluate the performance of our approach, multiple data sets were
used, beginning with a large set of urine samples inoculated with
bacterial cells (mimicking urinary tract infection (UTI)), that was
divided into training and validation subsets to develop a urine-specific
model. A second data set comprising patient urine samples infected
with various uropathogens was employed as a test set. To enhance the
model’s generalizability across different biological fluids,
supplementary data sets of plasma and semen from a public repository
were also incorporated, facilitating the development and evaluation
of a more broadly applicable model.
The training data for the
urine specific model was generated using a triple quadrupole TSQ Altis
mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) in Selected Reaction Monitoring
acquisition mode. A data set of multiple urine samples inoculated
with 12 different bacteria commonly responsible for Urinary Tract
Infections (UTIs) at 6 different concentrations was used. A previously
established peptide signature for the diagnosis of UTIs
25
was monitored, corresponding to 82 peptides
and 6 CytoC standards with 4 transitions each: transitions are specific
precursor–fragment-ion pairs for a given peptide. In total,
352 transitions were followed. Each sample also has 4 replicates for
optimal results giving a total of 288 samples. Full sample and spike
details can be found in Supporting Information (
Table S1
).
Bacterial cells were initially pelleted by
centrifugation and washed
with 50 mM Tris before being frozen on dry ice. Cell lysis involved
resuspending the pellet in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate with mutanolysin
enzyme, followed by incubation and subsequent inactivation of bacteria
cells and protein denaturation with sodium deoxycholate and DTT. Protein
digestion was achieved using trypsin enzyme, followed by acidification
with formic acid to halt digestion and precipitate SDC. Peptides in
the supernatant were purified, vacuum-dried, and stored for mass spectrometry
analysis. Peptide digests were prepared with 40fmol of DionexTM Cytochrome
C digest in 0.1% FA before injection onto a Vanquish Neo liquid chromatography
system with a 50 cm nanoPAC column. Elution occurred over 10 min from
5 to 50% solvent B (80% ACN/0.1% FA) at 2 μL/min. The system
was coupled to a TSQ-Altis mass spectrometer operating in SRM mode,
with parameters including a spray voltage of 1900 V and a heated ion
transfer tube at 275 °C.
For the machine learning process,
samples were split using urine
inoculated with 9 of the 12 bacteria as our training data set and
keeping the urine inoculated with the three remaining bacteria for
our validation data set. This provides a total of 216 samples for
training and 72 samples for testing hyperparameters as a validation
data set which corresponds to a 73/27% split. The raw output data
from mass spectrometer is preprocessed to be converted into a data
set ready to train a machine learning model. Finally, the model with
optimal hyperparameters is tested on independent patient samples that
underwent the same analysis. The patient data set used in this step
included a diverse selection of 84 urine samples representing typical
clinical presentations. Specifically, the data set encompasses samples
with various bacterial species commonly associated with urinary tract
infections, including
Escherichia coli
,
Klebsiella pneumoniae
,
Proteus mirabilis
,
Streptococcus agalactiae
,
Staphylococcus
saprophyticus
, and
Enterococcus faecalis
. Additionally, the samples exhibit a range of bacterial loads, from
10
4
to greater than 10
5
colony-forming units
(CFU) per mL, to evaluate model performance across different infection
intensities. All samples were collected as midstream urine to ensure
consistency in collection methods, while the samples were collected
across multiple dates to incorporate potential acquisition variability.
This diversity in bacterial species, concentration levels, and collection
timing is intended to provide a robust and comprehensive test set
for evaluating model generalizability and sensitivity. Further samples
of plasma semen, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from public repository
Panorama were later included to demonstrate the generalizability of
the model. Complete details of these data sets can be found in Supporting
Information (
Table S3
).
Preprocessing and Parsing of Raw Mass Spectrometry Data
First, the raw files are converted into mzXML files using ProteoWizard.
26
Then, the data is processed using a custom code
in R programming language.
27
Using this
code, the mzXML files are read and parsed using the MSnbase
28
library from Bioconductor.
29
The transition peak file, containing the sequence information
for each chosen transition of the experiment, is necessary at this
stage to correctly attribute the intensity values to the accurate
peptide sequence and transition. The first 30 lines of this file,
containing easily exportable information from Skyline, are available
in supplementary data (
Table S2
). The custom
R code then extracts the intensity for each transition of each precursor
at each time point throughout the run and formats all this information
into a CSV file with columns containing the precursor
m
/
z
value, the retention time, the sequence, the
intensity values for each transition and a final total intensity column
with the cumulative intensities of all transitions at the retention
time for all samples. This file containing in matrix form the values
of the chromatogram for each peptide in each sample, can be exported
in CSV format and serves as input for tracing the chromatogram for
each precursor in each sample. A separate R code is available to trace
these graphs using ggplot2
30
with the option
of applying a Savitzy-Golay smoothing filter, which is commonly used.
31
All the codes were adapted to be used
with mclapply in the parallel base R package (for use on a Linux server)
and doParallel (for use on Windows) for parallelization to optimize
computation time. These graphs are useful for visualizing the data
and allow for manual verification of the selected peaks when evaluating
the machine learning performance.
Feature Engineering
Three main criteria were established
to differentiate peptide peaks from other peaks in the chromatogram.
First, all transitions of the precursor should be present at the expected
window of retention time.
32
Second, the
peaks of each transition should have the same shape and maintain an
even ratio of intensity within the peak’s interval.
33
Third and finally, the peptide peak should be
distinct from the ambient noise within the chromatogram. However,
it is important to note that the peptide peak may not be the most
intense peak within the chromatogram and high-intensity interferences
may occur.
34
We sought to translate the
established criteria into machine learning features that algorithms
could use to perform automatic peak-picking.
A custom R code
is used that takes chromatogram CSV files containing each transition
intensity and calculates new features to serve as input for our machine
learning model. The function takes the previously calculated chromatogram
data for each precursor in each sample as input and gives the training
matrix for our machine learning model as output.

is the cumulative value of the intensity of each of the four transitions
for each precursor. For local maxima in the chromatogram, the function

In summary, the features
used by our machine learning model to
differentiate between true peptide peaks and false peaks arising from
noise or interference in the chromatogram include geometric mean,
z-scores, and scaled percentage and proportion metrics. Our custom
code performs detailed peak analysis and characterization within the
chromatogram data set, focusing on proportions and percentages that
define the shape and transition ratios of each peak—criteria
deemed critical during our research phase. Z-scores, which reflect
the intensity of each peak and transition relative to ambient noise,
are another key criterion for accurate peak identification. The geometric
mean further aids the model in distinguishing genuine peaks from noise,
particularly for peaks with lower intensity. These criteria are distilled
into 62 features: 28 PeakPercentages and 28 PeakProportions (derived
from 7 time points across 4 transitions), along with 5 z-scores (one
for each transition, one for total intensity), and a final geometric
mean. The final training matrix is organized with rows representing
each potential peptide peak (local maxima of total intensity) in the
chromatogram, and 63 columns that include one ID column alongside
the 62 feature columns. This comprehensive feature set captures diverse
aspects of peak characterization such as peak shape, intensity, and
transition dynamics. These features are specifically designed to enhance
the distinction between true peptide peaks and noise, forming the
basis of our machine learning model’s training and ensuring
robust differentiation between genuine peptide peaks and false signals.
Manual Labeling of Peaks in Training Data
To label
the training data, each chromatogram had to be manually annotated
to ensure correct peak identification. This was done by visually inspecting
the peaks and indicating the start and end time of the correct peak
in each chromatogram using the previously established criteria. For
ease, the Skyline interface was used to visualize and manually indicate
the peak boundaries which were exported as start and end times for
each peptide in each sample. These start and end times are compiled
in the Peak Boundaries file that can easily be exported (
Table S4
). Using the times present in the Peak
Boundaries file, the correct class label can be attributed to each
peak depending on whether the time of the maximum of the peak is within
the peak boundaries for that precursor. If the maximum of the peak
is at a time within the peak boundary for the precursor the class
label is given the value “TRUE”, if not it is attributed
the value “FALSE”. Further manual correction was applied
in the case of ambiguity of the correct peak within the peak boundaries.
These class labels are compiled in the final column of our data set:
the class column. Due to the nature of the data, there are more false
peaks than true peaks as, within a given chromatogram, there is at
most one true peptide peak, whereas there may be multiple local maxima
corresponding to noise of high intensity interference from coeluting
peptides. This disparity leads to an imbalanced data set, which is
a crucial factor to consider in our choice of model and evaluation
metrics for the machine learning phase. In our training and test data,
there is an average ratio of 1 True to 300 False overall.
Machine Learning
H2O.ai’s AutoML tool in R was
used to test multiple models using our 62 engineered features. H2O.ai’s
AutoML is a machine learning automation tool designed to streamline
the development process. It automates algorithm selection and parameter
tuning while exploring a diverse range of algorithms. These include
Gradient Boosted Machines (GBM), which build an ensemble of decision
trees sequentially to improve predictive performance; Generalized
Linear Models (GLM), which generalize linear regression to accommodate
different types of response variables; Directed Random Forests (DRF),
an ensemble learning method using multiple decision trees to enhance
accuracy and robustness; Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), an advanced
boosting method known for its high performance and efficiency; and
Deep Neural Networks (DNN), which use multiple layers of neurons to
model complex patterns in data. Cross-validation is used for individual
model tuning and evaluation. AutoML generates a leaderboard of models
and facilitates easy export of models. We ran AutoML using 10-fold
cross-validation and limited the AutoML process run time by determining
a maximum of 30 models in the leaderboard. The Area Under the Precision-Recall
Curve (AUPRC) was specified as the stopping metric because it is the
best of the available metrics for imbalanced data sets as is our case.
36
,
37
AUPRC is a single number that summarizes the information in the
precision-recall (PR) curve, which shows the trade-off between precision
and recall across different decision thresholds. The AUPRC formula
can be written as
where precision(
r
) is the
interpolated precision at recall level
r
. The AUPRC
varies between 0 and 1 and can be used as a performance metric for
imbalanced data in binary classification tasks. A higher AUPRC value
indicates better model performance in terms of both precision and
recall. Ideally, the Mathews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) would be
used as this is the preferred metric for evaluation of classification
models,
38
,
39
but this is not a readily available option
in H
2
O as a stopping metric. However, for comparison of
models in the leaderboard the MCC is used.
The MCC formula can
be written as
where TP corresponds to the number of True
Positives, TN corresponds to the number of True Negatives, FP corresponds
to the number of False Positives, and FN corresponds to the number
of False Negatives. A True Positive is, in our case, a peak that is
a true peptide peak and that the model correctly identifies as True.
A False Positive is a false peak that is mistakenly classified by
the model as True. A True Negative is a false peak that the model
correctly identifies as False. Finally, a False Negative is a true
peptide peak that the model mistakenly classifies as False. These
values can be summarized in a table referred to as a confusion matrix.
For evaluation of the leaderboard, performance was assessed on
cross-validation of the training data, The MCC was calculated for
each model and the leaderboard was ordered accordingly. The ordered
leaderboard is available in Supporting Information (
Table S5
) with further details on the tested algorithms. The
model with the best performance underwent further hyperparameter testing.
The hyperparameters with the highest performance on the validation
data set of urine was selected as our final best model.
Validation on Patient Urinary Tract Infection Data
To assess the accuracy of our model in a concrete use-case the highest
performing model was applied to the test data set of patient urine
samples tested for UTIs. Our model performs peak analysis, and the
results are compared to those obtained from the same data set using
mProphet, which was set with a detection
Q
-value
of 0.01 and no manual correction. We evaluate and compare the results
from both tools against manually assigned correct labels, using the
Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) as the scoring metric to ensure
a fair comparison.
Generalizable Model Training
To demonstrate the generalizability
of the ProPickML methodology beyond the application to Urinary Tract
Infections, a secondary model was trained with additional data. Using
the same model type and hyperparameters, a secondary XGBoost model
was trained on the previously used urine training data set along with
two data sets from public repositories. The first of these data sets
is from a study of semen samples from healthy men, and men recovering
from COVID-19, which include samples from 27 individuals (10 healthy
fertile controls and 17 COVID-19 recovered males), 54 peptides (1
heavy, 53 light) and 399 transitions.
40
The second data set is from a study of plasma samples from healthy
patients and patients with severe and nonsevere cases of COVID-19.
41
This study includes 12 (6 severe and 6 non severe)
COVID plasma samples with two bioreplicates, 29 peptides (1 heavy,
28 light) and 183 transitions. Data from all data sets were preprocessed
following the previously described steps and combined to form a large
general training data set. To assess the performance of the trained
general model, it was tested on the previously described patient urine
samples and on three test sets from public repository Panorama. The
second test set is from a longitudinal study of plasma samples in
patients at differing stages of COVID-19 severity.
42
The plasma data set includes 14 replicates, 7 peptides
(1 heavy, 6 light) and 45 transitions. The final test sets are from
the study of biomarkers of brain tumors from patients with gliomas
and meningiomas.
43
The cerebrospinal fluid
data set includes 10 replicates, 15 peptides and 64 transitions for
glioma patients and 7 replicates, 15 peptides and 62 transitions for
meningioma patients. All data sets were preprocessed following the
previously described steps (Figure
1
).

Our method involves three major steps: data acquisition, feature engineering
and data preproduction and finally, training of the machine learning

Introduction
In LC-MS-based proteomics, untargeted
proteomics involves the analysis
of all proteins in a sample without predefining the targets allowing
for numerous applications such as the discovery of new proteins and
biomarkers.
1
In targeted proteomics, specific
proteins are identified and quantified using mass spectrometry techniques.
The choice between targeted and untargeted proteomics depends on the
research goals and the nature of the study.
Targeted proteomics
has become a veritable cornerstone in biomedical
research, evolving in diverse applications such as biomarker validation,
relative or absolute quantification in biofluids. The technique has
aided in elucidating biological functions and disorders such as autism
2
and cancer,
3
contributes
to systems biology research,
4
aids in metabolic
engineering optimization,
5
characterizes
human bodily fluids and tissues
6
and validates
biomarkers with high accuracy.
7
,
8
This technique’s
versatility and precision make it indispensable across a range of
disciplines, driving advancements in therapeutics, personalized medicine,
and diagnostics.
In diagnostics, targeted proteomics is emerging
as a compelling
alternative to traditional antibody-based methods. While antibodies
have been conventionally employed for protein detection, they often
face limitations such as cross-reactivity
9
and batch-to-batch variability
10
while
also incurring high costs. In contrast, targeted proteomics offers
a more precise and reproducible approach
11
and allows for multiplexing which increases the number of samples
studied per analysis.
12
By directly measuring
specific protein targets using mass spectrometry, it circumvents antibody-related
challenges, providing high specificity and accuracy in diagnostic
assays. This alternative approach holds promise for overcoming issues
associated with antibody-based diagnostics, offering a reliable and
cost-effective avenue for improved and streamlined diagnostic procedures.
Targeted proteomics utilizes two main techniques: Parallel Reaction
Monitoring (PRM)
13
and Selected Reaction
Monitoring (SRM).
14
In both cases, target
proteins are digested using trypsin and broken into peptides that
are analyzed by the mass spectrometers to evaluate the intensity of
the peptides in various samples. PRM offers high resolution and high
precision but has a higher cost to use, both in terms of machinery
and the level of expertise for operation and maintenance, which limits
its accessibility for routine, high-throughput applications. On the
other hand, SRM has a lower price of entry using simpler, less expensive
machines that require less maintenance making it suitable for large-scale
studies. Recently, SRM machines have been approved for clinical use
providing a more accessible alternative to expensive PRM machines.
15
SRM has been successfully applied to the diagnosis
of cancer,
16
SARS-CoV-2,
17
pleural effusions in Cancer and tuberculosis.
18
However, SRM does have some drawbacks,
with its lower resolution
leading to numerous interferences, making the target peptide more
difficult to isolate.
19
During SRM, the
mass spectrometer selects a predefined precursor ion, fragments it,
and then selectively detects a specific product ion, allowing for
precise quantification of the target peptide. SRM isolates and monitors
specific precursor and product ion pairs corresponding to target peptides
using mass spectrometry, these precursor-ions parings are referred
to as transitions. For each peptide, multiple transitions are monitored
to increase specificity, yet interferences can occur when coeluting
compounds generate ions similar to the targeted peptide. These interferences
lead to challenges in distinguishing and accurately quantifying the
intended signal amid background noise, especially for low abundance
peptides in complex biological samples.
Solutions exist to mitigate
these problems, such as the use of
isotopically labeled peptides. Isotopic labeling involves synthesizing
marked versions of the target peptides, where stable isotopes are
included into the peptide sequence, creating a mass difference that
aids in distinguishing the target peptide from interfering species.
These marked peptides are then used as internal standards
20
in the samples, which enhances specificity and
reduces false positives, providing more reliable quantification. However,
a drawback of using isotopic labels is that this doubles the number
of peptides and transitions to monitor, which leads to longer run
times. Indeed, there is a trade-off between the cycle time and the
number of peptides being followed. As the number of peptides increases,
the cycle time for acquiring data for each peptide also rises.
21
This trade-off poses a challenge in balancing
the need to monitor high numbers of peptides with the practical constraints
of analysis time, especially in large-scale studies where a high number
of peptides are of interest. Researchers must carefully optimize these
parameters to achieve the desired sensitivity and throughput without
sacrificing analytical efficiency. Furthermore, while isotopically
labeled peptides are reasonably priced, they do contribute to elevating
the overall cost of SRM analysis. This, coupled with the necessity
to extend cycle times, offsets the advantages of the rapid run-time
and lower cost associated with using SRM for diagnosis. Automatic
scoring applications provide a valuable solution to the challenge
of accurately identifying peptide peaks in SRM analysis. These applications
calculate various features of given peaks and score their likelihood
of being the desired peptide. Skyline,
22
widely used for SRM analysis, employs mProphet
23
for scoring, which evaluates multiple parameters. However,
limitations arise, particularly in diagnostic applications when used
without isotopically labeled peptides, as mProphet tends to select
a peak even in the absence of the targeted peptide, resulting in a
high rate of false positives.
24
This issue
necessitates manual correction and refinement of peak boundaries,
hindering fully automated analysis. While other vendor algorithms
like Sciex’s MultiQuant and Thermo Fischer’s Tracefinder
also exist, they are not freely available and may introduce additional
costs.
Employing artificial intelligence-based approaches could
aid in
addressing the challenges in targeted proteomic analysis while maintaining
cost-effectiveness and high-throughput. To this end, we present a
novel, cost-free automated tool, ProPickML, that utilizes a pretrained
machine learning model. This model is specifically designed to automatically
identify peptide peaks and reduce the need for manual validation by
leveraging engineered features from the raw data. We aim to increase
performance when compared to current tools and introduce new measures
to characterize peptide peaks and distinguish them from noise and
interference. ProPickML was implemented and assessed in a practical
scenario, using a data set focused on diagnosing urinary tract infections
before extending analysis to multiple biological samples.

Feature Engineering
Three main criteria were established
to differentiate peptide peaks from other peaks in the chromatogram.
First, all transitions of the precursor should be present at the expected
window of retention time.
32
Second, the
peaks of each transition should have the same shape and maintain an
even ratio of intensity within the peak’s interval.
33
Third and finally, the peptide peak should be
distinct from the ambient noise within the chromatogram. However,
it is important to note that the peptide peak may not be the most
intense peak within the chromatogram and high-intensity interferences
may occur.
34
We sought to translate the
established criteria into machine learning features that algorithms
could use to perform automatic peak-picking.
A custom R code
is used that takes chromatogram CSV files containing each transition
intensity and calculates new features to serve as input for our machine
learning model. The function takes the previously calculated chromatogram
data for each precursor in each sample as input and gives the training
matrix for our machine learning model as output.

total time points of our potential peptide peaks that will be classified
by our machine learning model. Features called transition proportions

In summary, the features
used by our machine learning model to
differentiate between true peptide peaks and false peaks arising from
noise or interference in the chromatogram include geometric mean,
z-scores, and scaled percentage and proportion metrics. Our custom
code performs detailed peak analysis and characterization within the
chromatogram data set, focusing on proportions and percentages that
define the shape and transition ratios of each peak—criteria
deemed critical during our research phase. Z-scores, which reflect
the intensity of each peak and transition relative to ambient noise,
are another key criterion for accurate peak identification. The geometric
mean further aids the model in distinguishing genuine peaks from noise,
particularly for peaks with lower intensity. These criteria are distilled
into 62 features: 28 PeakPercentages and 28 PeakProportions (derived
from 7 time points across 4 transitions), along with 5 z-scores (one
for each transition, one for total intensity), and a final geometric
mean. The final training matrix is organized with rows representing
each potential peptide peak (local maxima of total intensity) in the
chromatogram, and 63 columns that include one ID column alongside
the 62 feature columns. This comprehensive feature set captures diverse
aspects of peak characterization such as peak shape, intensity, and
transition dynamics. These features are specifically designed to enhance
the distinction between true peptide peaks and noise, forming the
basis of our machine learning model’s training and ensuring
robust differentiation between genuine peptide peaks and false signals.
Manual Labeling of Peaks in Training Data
To label
the training data, each chromatogram had to be manually annotated
to ensure correct peak identification. This was done by visually inspecting
the peaks and indicating the start and end time of the correct peak
in each chromatogram using the previously established criteria. For
ease, the Skyline interface was used to visualize and manually indicate
the peak boundaries which were exported as start and end times for
each peptide in each sample. These start and end times are compiled
in the Peak Boundaries file that can easily be exported (
Table S4
). Using the times present in the Peak
Boundaries file, the correct class label can be attributed to each
peak depending on whether the time of the maximum of the peak is within
the peak boundaries for that precursor. If the maximum of the peak
is at a time within the peak boundary for the precursor the class
label is given the value “TRUE”, if not it is attributed
the value “FALSE”. Further manual correction was applied
in the case of ambiguity of the correct peak within the peak boundaries.
These class labels are compiled in the final column of our data set:
the class column. Due to the nature of the data, there are more false
peaks than true peaks as, within a given chromatogram, there is at
most one true peptide peak, whereas there may be multiple local maxima
corresponding to noise of high intensity interference from coeluting
peptides. This disparity leads to an imbalanced data set, which is
a crucial factor to consider in our choice of model and evaluation
metrics for the machine learning phase. In our training and test data,
there is an average ratio of 1 True to 300 False overall.
Machine Learning
H2O.ai’s AutoML tool in R was
used to test multiple models using our 62 engineered features. H2O.ai’s
AutoML is a machine learning automation tool designed to streamline
the development process. It automates algorithm selection and parameter
tuning while exploring a diverse range of algorithms. These include
Gradient Boosted Machines (GBM), which build an ensemble of decision
trees sequentially to improve predictive performance; Generalized
Linear Models (GLM), which generalize linear regression to accommodate
different types of response variables; Directed Random Forests (DRF),
an ensemble learning method using multiple decision trees to enhance
accuracy and robustness; Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), an advanced
boosting method known for its high performance and efficiency; and
Deep Neural Networks (DNN), which use multiple layers of neurons to
model complex patterns in data. Cross-validation is used for individual
model tuning and evaluation. AutoML generates a leaderboard of models
and facilitates easy export of models. We ran AutoML using 10-fold
cross-validation and limited the AutoML process run time by determining
a maximum of 30 models in the leaderboard. The Area Under the Precision-Recall
Curve (AUPRC) was specified as the stopping metric because it is the
best of the available metrics for imbalanced data sets as is our case.

,
37

precision-recall (PR) curve, which shows the trade-off between precision
and recall across different decision thresholds. The AUPRC formula

A False Positive is a false peak that is mistakenly classified by

For evaluation of the leaderboard, performance was assessed on

The hyperparameters with the highest performance on the validation
data set of urine was selected as our final best model.
Validation on Patient Urinary Tract Infection Data
To assess the accuracy of our model in a concrete use-case the highest
performing model was applied to the test data set of patient urine
samples tested for UTIs. Our model performs peak analysis, and the
results are compared to those obtained from the same data set using
mProphet, which was set with a detection
Q
-value
of 0.01 and no manual correction. We evaluate and compare the results
from both tools against manually assigned correct labels, using the
Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) as the scoring metric to ensure
a fair comparison.

To demonstrate the generalizability
of the ProPickML methodology beyond the application to Urinary Tract
Infections, a secondary model was trained with additional data. Using
the same model type and hyperparameters, a secondary XGBoost model
was trained on the previously used urine training data set along with
two data sets from public repositories. The first of these data sets
is from a study of semen samples from healthy men, and men recovering

The second data set is from a study of plasma samples from healthy

Identification of the Highest Performing Model
The
top ten best nonensemble models from the H2O AutoML leaderboard are
all extreme Gradient Boosting models (XGBoost). XGBoost (Extreme Gradient
Boosting) is a machine learning algorithm that enhances the gradient
boosting framework by building decision trees sequentially, each aimed
at correcting the errors of the previous ones. It optimizes the loss
function using both first-order (gradient) and second-order (Hessian)
derivatives. XGBoost includes L1 and L2 regularization to prevent
overfitting, and it efficiently handles missing and sparse data. The
algorithm supports parallel processing for faster training and employs
tree pruning techniques to maintain model simplicity. These principles
make XGBoost a highly accurate, scalable, and efficient tool for predictive
modeling.
44
To achieve maximum performance,
a secondary step of grid search on XGBoost models only using the xgboost
R package was performed.

Discussion
In this manuscript, we have provided a new
approach for the processing
of SRM data based on a trained machine learning model that has improved
performances of the current methods (peak scoring) to distinguish
between true peptide peaks, and false peaks that are noise or interferences,
without manual intervention. Although our model has been developed
for the diagnosis of UTIs, we demonstrated its applicability on other
data sets (plasma, semen, cerebrospinal fluid) paving the way for
its future use in a broader clinical context.
Our model is based
on engineered features created using the insight
of experienced skilled professionals. A simple analysis shows the
capacity of these features to accurately distinguish between true
peptide peaks and false peaks. We hope these features will provide
further insight into the characterization of peptide peaks in chromatograms
and may form the basis of further research.
Moreover, as artificial
intelligence becomes increasingly indispensable
across various fields, including biological data processing, ProPickML
stands as the first tool to employ a pretrained AI model for peak
detection in SRM, addressing the well-known challenge of interferences
in mass spectrometry analyses. This proof of concept not only demonstrates
the efficacy of AI in improving the accuracy and efficiency of SRM
data interpretation but also opens the door for AI’s broader
application in combination with mass spectrometry, particularly in
diagnostic settings where high-throughput analysis is required. For
instance, clinical microbiology laboratories often process hundreds
of urine samples daily, necessitating rapid and reliable automated
tools. ProPickML’s approach can be further refined with additional
data sets and extended to other types of mass spectrometry data, such
as PRM and DIA, enhancing its performance and versatility.
Concerning
the choice of an XGBoost model, the model was chosen
after testing various other models in the AutoML tool of H2O. Various
other AutoML tools were also tested, such as BioDiscML,
46
a biomarker discovery software that uses the
Weka 3.8 machine learning library to automate model training and feature
selection. BiodiscML confirmed that tree type models were the most
pertinent to solve our classification problem. Knowing this, forester,
47
an R based AutoML tool specialized in tree type
models, was also tested, however, H2O models had the best overall
performance of all models from all the tested AutoMLs. The consensus
of multiple tools does lend itself to the conclusion that tree type
models seem to be the model type most adapted to peak analysis in
this case. However, XGBoost is only available within H2O and constituted
the top ten models in the H2O leaderboard demonstrating that it is
the preferred model type for our classification problem. Knowing this
we chose to do further fine-tuning of XGBoost models using the xgboost
44
package directly.
Our Urine Specific model
currently has an MCC of 0.81 and an FDR
of 0.09 on the independent test data set of patient samples. These
results show the potential of machine learning models to solve the
complex issue of automatizing peak-picking in diagnosis workflows.
Manual curation presents its own limits of precision and reproducibility,
and although complete accuracy has not yet been achieved, we believe
there is a viable trade-off between speed of analysis and precision
when using a machine learning model for peak picking. However, users
are urged to evaluate the validity of this trade-off in their particular
use case.
We also demonstrated that our model is generalizable
and performs
well on both plasma and urine samples, indicating that our features
and methodology are effective across different sample types and peptides.
Each data set originates from distinct studies and repositories, containing
various peptides and differing numbers of transitions. Nonetheless,
we acknowledge that our current data originates from only two research
groups, which could have an impact on generalizability across other
laboratories or protocols. Furthermore, to ensure model stability,
we limited the number of transitions to four for samples with more
than four transitions. Performance on these data sets demonstrated
that using information from just four transitions was sufficient for
accurate peak classification. However, for optimal performance of
ProPickML we encourage users to select the four best transitions for
their specific data set if that information is available to them.
ProPickML has the advantage of being a standalone, flexible solution
based on simple, generalizable features. More complex features, such
as calculating derivatives, integrating all peaks, and evaluating
the Gaussian fit could potentially increase the performance of the
model. However, such features come with a high computational cost
when accounting for the large number of peaks to be evaluated which
could significantly increase the time necessary for analysis and limit
its generalization to many data sets. Further analysis and development
are necessary to perfect the use of machine learning models and eliminate
manual verification completely.
When investigating the errors
currently made by our model, they
are mainly false negatives, which is to say true peptide peaks that
are classified as false. When investigating these errors further,
the majority of these misclassified peaks had low intensities compared
to the intensity of noise and interference in the chromatogram. The
performance of ProPickML in such cases was comparable with mProphet
that also misclassified these peaks as false. It is possible that
low-intensity peptides may require specific peak characterization
to accurately distinguish them. Further work on a specialized model
for noisy, low-intensity data sets with new features could be an avenue
to improve performance in this area.
Overall, ProPickML represents
a proof of concept for the use of
AI in the processing of SRM data. We have demonstrated it exceeds
the current peak scoring-based gold standard in terms of both accuracy
and false discovery rate. Moreover, it relies on generalizable and
nonspecific features and can therefore be applied to other data sets.
In future work, the performance and generalizability of our methodology
can be improved even more by continuing to apply it to multiple data
sets to provide an even more generalizable solution to accelerate
peak analysis in a reproducible and precise manner. A potential next
step would be a large-scale model trained on all targeted proteomics
data sets available in the Panorama repository, however this would
require considerable computational and storage resources to preprocess
and include all data sets in a large training model.
